response.question: Someone is selling products with my registered trademark on them. What can I do?
response.answer:
Selling products with your registered trade mark may be infringement, but it depends on the circumstances. For example, the law covers unauthorised use in trade of an identical or deceptively similar mark on goods for which the mark is registered. Offering goods for sale under the mark counts as use. Not every sale is infringement. For example, there are limits on infringement claims involving lawfully acquired goods put on the market under the mark by you or with your consent. [trade_marks_act_1999:30]

A court may grant an injunction—an order to stop certain conduct—and may also award damages or an account of profits. These remedies are not automatic. [trade_marks_act_1999:135]

response.question: Why could my trademark application be rejected?
response.answer:
Your application could be refused for several reasons. The reason in your case depends on your mark, your goods or services, and any earlier rights.

• Your mark does not distinguish your goods or services from others, or consists only of descriptive or commonly used terms. But this may not apply if the mark became distinctive through use before you applied, or is well known. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]

• Your mark could deceive or confuse the public; contains material likely to hurt religious sensitivities, or scandalous or obscene material; or is prohibited under the law mentioned in the source. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]

• Your mark consists only of a goods shape that results from the nature of the goods, is necessary for a technical result, or gives the goods substantial value. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]

• Your mark is identical or similar to an earlier mark, and the goods or services are also identical or similar, creating a likelihood of public confusion or association. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

• Your mark conflicts with a well-known Indian mark, even for different goods or services, if the conditions in the source are met. Use of your mark may also be prevented by rights protecting an unregistered mark or by copyright. These grounds cannot be used to refuse registration unless the proprietor of the earlier mark raises an objection in opposition proceedings. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

• The Registrar may also accept an application subject to changes, conditions or limits. If the application is refused or accepted with conditions, the Registrar must record the reasons and materials used in writing. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]

response.question: How long is a trademark registration valid and how do I renew it?
response.answer:
A trade mark registered after the Trade Marks Act came into force is valid for 10 years. It can be renewed repeatedly, for 10 years at a time. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

To renew, the registered owner must apply to the Registrar in the prescribed manner and period and pay the prescribed fee. The sources provided do not specify the usual application deadline, form or fee amount. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

If the registration has expired, an application in the prescribed form, with the fee and a surcharge, can be made within six months of expiry. If the mark has been removed for non-payment, restoration can be requested after six months and within one year of expiry. Restoration is subject to the Registrar being satisfied that it is just to restore it. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

An international registration at the International Bureau also lasts 10 years and can be renewed for successive 10-year periods. A six-month grace period is available subject to a surcharge. [trade_marks_act_1999:36G]

response.question: How long does copyright last for a book after the author dies?
response.answer:
For a book published during the author’s lifetime, copyright generally lasts 60 years, counted from 1 January of the year after the author dies. For example, if the author died in 2000, the term runs until the end of 2060. [copyright_act_1957:22]

If the book has joint authors, the period is counted from the year after the last author dies. [copyright_act_1957:22]

Different rules can apply. For example, if the book and its adaptations were not published before the author’s death, and copyright existed at death, the 60 years generally runs from the year after first publication. An earlier publication of an adaptation can change the starting point. [copyright_act_1957:24] Books published anonymously or under a pen name can also follow a different rule. [copyright_act_1957:23]

response.question: My employer says they own the articles I wrote at work. Who owns the copyright?
response.answer:
It depends on your employment, what the articles were written for, and any agreement you have with your employer.

If you wrote the articles in the course of your employment under an employment or apprenticeship contract, your employer is generally the first copyright owner, unless you agreed otherwise. A special rule applies to certain newspaper and magazine employees. [copyright_act_1957:17]

If you worked for the owner of a newspaper, magazine or similar periodical and wrote the articles for publication there, the owner is generally the first owner of the rights to publish them in such periodicals or reproduce them for that purpose. You are generally the first owner of the other copyright rights, unless you agreed otherwise. [copyright_act_1957:17]

These are rules about the first owner. Copyright can also be transferred, wholly or partly, so any relevant agreement matters. [copyright_act_1957:18]

response.question: Someone copied my book and is selling it. What legal action can I take?
response.answer:
If you own the copyright and the copies are infringing, you may have a civil claim. Selling infringing copies can itself be copyright infringement [copyright_act_1957:51].

You can ask a court for an injunction—an order to stop the infringement—and seek damages (money for loss) or an account of profits [copyright_act_1957:55]. If the seller proves they did not know and had no reasonable grounds to believe copyright existed in the work, the available remedies are limited: an injunction and, if the court considers it reasonable, all or part of the profits from selling the infringing copies [copyright_act_1957:55].

You may also bring proceedings to recover possession of infringing copies and equipment used or intended to produce them [copyright_act_1957:58]. Whether the copies infringe will depend on the facts; some uses are exceptions, including certain fair dealing for criticism or review [copyright_act_1957:52].

response.question: What is the jail punishment for copyright piracy?

For knowingly infringing copyright, or helping someone else do so, the usual punishment is 6 months to 3 years in jail, plus a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh.

A separate provision applies to knowingly using an infringing copy of a computer program: the usual punishment is 7 days to 3 years in jail, plus a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. If the program was not used for gain or in the course of trade or business, the court may give no jail sentence and impose a fine of up to ₹50,000, for adequate and special reasons recorded in the judgment.

response.question: Can someone challenge or oppose my patent?
response.answer:
Yes. Someone can oppose a patent at different stages:

• Before grant: Once your application is published, but before the patent is granted, any person can submit a written opposition to the Controller, the patent authority. [patents_act_1970:25]

• After grant: A person interested can give notice of opposition to the Controller after grant but before one year expires from the date the grant was published. [patents_act_1970:25] A person interested includes someone engaged in or promoting research in the same field. [patents_act_1970:2]

Possible grounds include wrongful obtaining of the invention, earlier publication, obviousness, or an insufficiently clear description of the invention. These are examples, not the complete list. [patents_act_1970:25]

For a post-grant opposition, the Controller notifies the patent holder and refers the opposition to an Opposition Board. After receiving its recommendation and giving both sides an opportunity to be heard, the Controller may maintain, amend or revoke the patent. [patents_act_1970:25]

response.question: What exclusive rights does copyright give me over my novel?

- Make a film or sound recording based on it. [copyright_act_1957:14]
- Translate it. [copyright_act_1957:14]
- Adapt it, meaning rework it into another form. [copyright_act_1957:14]
- Exercise these rights in relation to a translation or adaptation too. [copyright_act_1957:14]

These rights apply to the whole novel or a substantial part of it, and are subject to the Act’s provisions. [copyright_act_1957:14]

response.question: Is it a crime to sell fake branded goods?
response.answer:
Yes. Selling goods with a false trade mark or false trade description can be a crime. This can include goods bearing a brand’s mark, or a confusingly similar mark, applied without the brand owner’s consent. [trade_marks_act_1999:104; trade_marks_act_1999:102]

A seller may avoid punishment if they prove, for example, that they took all reasonable precautions and had no reason to suspect a problem; that they gave the prosecutor all the information they had about their supplier when asked; or that they otherwise acted innocently. [trade_marks_act_1999:104]

The punishment is generally six months to three years in prison and a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. A court may impose a lower prison term or fine for adequate and special reasons recorded in its judgment. [trade_marks_act_1999:104]

response.question: What rights do I get once my patent is granted?
response.answer:
A granted patent gives you the right to stop others from doing certain things in India without your permission:

• For a product patent, you can stop others from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the product for those purposes. [patents_act_1970:48]
• For a process patent, you can stop others from using the process, and from using, offering for sale, selling or importing for those purposes a product obtained directly by that process. [patents_act_1970:48]

These rights have limits. For example, the Government may make or import a patented article or use a patented process for its own use. A person may also make or use a patented article or use a patented process for experiment or research, including teaching pupils. [patents_act_1970:47]

If you have co-owners, different rules apply: for example, unless an agreement says otherwise, each owner generally has an equal undivided share. Consent from the other owners is generally needed to license the patent or transfer an owner's share, subject to any agreement in force. [patents_act_1970:50]

response.question: A company copied my patented invention. What can a court order against them?
response.answer:
In a patent infringement suit, a court can grant an injunction—an order requiring a party to stop specified activity. It can also award damages (money for loss) or an account of profits (a financial remedy based on profits). These remedies are not automatic. [patents_act_1970:111; patents_act_1970:109]

There are limits on the money remedies. For example, neither damages nor an account of profits can be granted if the company proves that, when the infringement occurred, it did not know and had no reasonable grounds to believe that the patent existed. The court may also refuse these remedies for infringement during certain periods following a missed renewal fee. Special restrictions can apply to use before an amendment to the patent specification was allowed. These restrictions do not remove the court’s power to grant an injunction. [patents_act_1970:111]
